의미를 왜곡하는 맥락에서 사진을 게시하고 재판매, 부분 복제, 변조 또는 다른 이미지에 통합하는 것과 같은 사진의 모든 수정, 자료를 제3자에게 제공하는 것은 대한민국정부(운영자/저작권자)의 명시적인 허가 없이 금지됩니다.

yi_sun_sin.description: Bust of Yi held at the War Memorial of Korea. Note that this is a modern reconstruction of what he looked like; there are no known surviving contemporary depictions of him. The KOGL license for this image is visible when you search for this page in their internal search engine of the War Memorial website. Also displayed here: [1]. Unfortunately I can't find info on who created this sculpture, but whatever the case it's clearly in the collection of the War Memorial and copyright is consistently attributed to them.

darwin.description: Photograph of Charles Darwin; the frontispiece of Francis Darwin's The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (1887) has the caption "From a Photograph (1854?) by Messrs. Maull. And Fox. Engraved for Harper's Magazine, October 1884."[1]  In an 1899 paper, Francis Darwin wrote that "The date of the photograph is probably 1854; it is, however, impossible to be certain on this point, the books of Messrs. Maull and Fox having been destroyed by fire. The reproduction is by Mr. Dew-Smith, who has been at some disadvantage, having only an old and faded print to work from."[2]

thoreau.description: Portrait photograph from a ninth-plate daguerreotype of Henry David Thoreau. Calvin R. Greene was a Thoreau “disciple” who lived in Rochester, Michigan, and who first began corresponding with Thoreau in January 1856.  When Greene asked for a photographic image of the author, Thoreau initially replied: “You may rely on it that you have the best of me in my books, and that I am not worth seeing personally – the stuttering, blundering, clodhopper that I am.” Yet Greene repeated his request and sent money for the sitting.  Thoreau must have kept this commitment to his fan in the back of his mind for the next several months.  On June 18, 1856, during a trip to Worcester, Massachusetts, Henry Thoreau visited the Daguerrean Palace of Benjamin D. Maxham at 16 Harrington Corner and had three daguerreotypes taken for fifty cents each.  He gave two of the prints to his Worcester friends and hosts, H.G.O. Blake and Theophilius Brown.  The third he sent to Calvin Greene in Michigan.  “While in Worcester this week I obtained the accompanying daguerreotype – which my friends think is pretty good – though better looking than I,” Thoreau wrote.
